title: Question 2
stem:
A small charged glass bead of weight $5.4 \times 10^{-5} \text{N}$ is initially at rest at point A in a vacuum. The bead then falls through a uniform horizontal electric field as it moves in a straight line to point B, as illustrated in Fig. 2.1.

{{figure:figure_2_1}}

Fig. 2.1 (not to scale)

The electric field strength is $1.3 \times 10^{4} \text{V m}^{-1}$. The charge on the bead is $-3.7 \times 10^{-9} \text{C}$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Describe how two metal plates could be used to produce the electric field. Numerical values are not required.

markscheme_points.text: left plate positively charged and right plate negatively charged/earthed or right plate negatively charged and left plate positively charged/earthed

hints: Hint 1: Think about what arrangement of plates gives field lines that are parallel, equally spaced and horizontal. What orientation must the plates themselves have?
Hint 2: Remember field direction is from positive to negative. The bead is negative and is pushed to the left in the diagram, so which way must the field point and which plate must be positive?
parts.proper_answer: Place two parallel metal plates vertically with a separation between them. Charge the left-hand plate positively and the right-hand plate negatively (or earthed) to give a uniform horizontal field directed to the right.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **How to make a uniform field**
You get a uniform field in the region between two parallel metal plates connected to a potential difference. The field lines are straight, parallel and equally spaced, and they run at right angles to the plates. For a horizontal field, the plates must be vertical and face each other.

Step 2: **Choosing the polarity**
Electric field direction is defined as the direction a positive charge would be pushed, from positive to negative. Here the bead has charge $-3.7 \times 10^{-9} \text{ C}$ and the path AB bends to the left, so the electric force on it is to the left. Because the charge is negative, force and field are in opposite directions, so the field must point to the right. That means the left plate is positive and the right plate is negative.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Determine the magnitude of the electric force acting on the bead.
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the two numbers given for the field region: field strength $E$ and charge $Q$ on the bead. Recall how field strength is defined in terms of force on a charge.
Hint 2: Check you use the magnitude of the charge and give the answer in newtons to 2 significant figures.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Linking field, charge and force**
Field strength tells you how much force each coulomb of charge feels. That is $$E = \frac{F}{Q}$$ so rearranged $$F = EQ$$ The field is uniform, so this force has the same value everywhere between the plates.

Step 2: **Putting in the numbers**
Use the magnitude of the charge: $$F = (1.3 \times 10^{4}) \times (3.7 \times 10^{-9})$$ $$F = 4.81 \times 10^{-5} \text{ N} \approx 4.8 \times 10^{-5} \text{ N}$$ This force acts horizontally.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Use your answer in (b) and the weight of the bead to show that the resultant force acting on it is $7.2 \times 10^{-5} \text{N}$.
hints: Hint 1: Draw the two forces tail-to-tail: weight vertically down and electric force horizontally. Since they are at right angles, think about which rule combines them into the hypotenuse.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Combining at right angles**
Weight acts vertically down and the electric force acts horizontally, so they are perpendicular. The resultant is the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle: $$F_{res}^{2} = F_{electric}^{2} + W^{2}$$ $$F_{res} = \sqrt{(4.8 \times 10^{-5})^{2} + (5.4 \times 10^{-5})^{2}}$$ $$F_{res} \approx 7.2 \times 10^{-5} \text{ N}$$ This resultant points along AB, which is why the bead moves in a straight line.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Explain why the resultant force on the bead of $7.2 \times 10^{-5} \text{N}$ is constant as the bead moves along path AB.

markscheme_points.text: electric force is constant (because field strength/E is constant)
weight is constant (and so resultant force constant)

hints: Hint 1: Think about what stays the same as the bead falls: the field strength $E$ at different positions, and the charge $Q$ on the bead.
Hint 2: Think about the other contributor to the resultant, the weight $W = mg$, and whether mass or $g$ change over this short fall.
parts.proper_answer: The electric field is uniform so $E$ is constant, hence electric force $F = EQ$ is constant. Weight $W = mg$ is also constant, so the vector sum of two constant perpendicular forces is constant in magnitude and direction.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why the electric part is constant**
In a uniform field the field strength $E$ is the same at every point. The charge $Q$ on the bead does not change, so $$F = EQ$$ stays constant in magnitude and horizontal direction all along AB.

Step 2: **Why the total is constant**
Weight $W = mg$ depends only on mass and gravitational field strength, both constant over the 0.58 m fall. Adding two constant vectors, one horizontal and one vertical, always gives the same resultant vector. Constant resultant force is exactly what produces straight-line motion from rest along AB.

parts.label: (e)(i)
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the acceleration of the bead along the path AB.
hints: Hint 1: You know the weight and the resultant force, but Newton's second law needs mass. Recall how weight and mass are linked.
Hint 2: Once mass is known, apply $F = ma$ using the resultant force along AB, since acceleration is in the same direction as the resultant.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Finding the mass first**
Weight and mass are different: weight is a force. $$W = mg$$ so $$m = \frac{W}{g} = \frac{5.4 \times 10^{-5}}{9.81} \approx 5.5 \times 10^{-6} \text{ kg}$$

Step 2: **Using Newton second law along AB**
Resultant force causes acceleration along the same line AB: $$F = ma$$ $$a = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{7.2 \times 10^{-5}}{5.5 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 13 \text{ m s}^{-2}$$

parts.label: (e)(ii)
parts.text:
The path AB has length $0.58 \text{m}$.

Use your answer in (i) to determine the speed of the bead at point B.
hints: Hint 1: List what you have along the slope AB: initial speed $u = 0$ since it starts from rest, acceleration $a$ from (i), distance $s = 0.58 \text{ m}$. Which SUVAT equation links these to final speed $v$ without time?
Hint 2: Remember to take the square root at the end and keep units as $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choosing the motion equation**
Acceleration along AB is constant, so the SUVAT equations apply along that line. Starting from rest means $u = 0$. With $s$ and $a$ known but $t$ unknown, use: $$v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as$$

Step 2: **Calculating the speed at B**
$$v^{2} = 0 + 2 \times 13 \times 0.58$$ $$v = \sqrt{15.1} \approx 3.9 \text{ m s}^{-1}$$ This is the speed directed along AB at point B.
